drapeaux.note: Verified word for word in the Review Board decision of February 14, 2022 (copyright.gov PDF), whose sentence reads: "After reviewing the statutory text, judicial precedent, and longstanding Copyright Office practice, the Board again concludes that human authorship is a prerequisite to copyright protection in the United States and that the Work therefore cannot be registered." The quotation keeps its second half. The Burrow-Giles definition is quoted verbatim as the Board cites it. The Howell phrase was corrected to the wording of the opinion text (Justia, D.D.C. Aug. 18, 2023): "sine qua non at the core of copyrightability".

titre: A machine cannot sign a work
accroche: In 2022, the Copyright Office refuses to register an image whose stated author is an artificial intelligence. The courts uphold the refusal through 2026.
contenu_vulgarise:
On November 3, 2018, computer scientist Stephen Thaler files an application with the U.S. Copyright Office to register an image titled A Recent Entrance to Paradise. In the author field, he enters not his own name but that of the Creativity Machine, the artificial intelligence system he built, which produced the image autonomously. Thaler presents himself as the owner of the machine, claiming copyright by transfer from it.

## A century of case law, a single answer

The Copyright Office refuses registration on August 12, 2019. Thaler asks for reconsideration twice; the agency's Review Board upholds the refusal on February 14, 2022. The decision rests on an 1884 precedent, Burrow-Giles Lithographic Co. v. Sarony, in which the Supreme Court defined an author as “he to whom anything owes its origin; originator; maker; one who completes a work of science or literature.” The Board concludes, after reviewing the text of the statute, the case law and its own practice: “the Board again concludes that human authorship is a prerequisite to copyright protection in the United States and that the Work therefore cannot be registered.”

Thaler takes the case to the federal courts. On August 18, 2023, Judge Beryl Howell of the D.C. district court upholds the refusal: human creativity, she writes, is the “sine qua non at the core of copyrightability.” The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit affirms in turn on March 18, 2025, ruling that human authorship is a substantive requirement of the Copyright Act, not just an administrative practice. On March 2, 2026, the Supreme Court declines to review the case any further, without giving a reason, the usual outcome of a denial of certiorari.

## What none of these decisions settles

None of these four bodies rules that a work made with the help of artificial intelligence is excluded from copyright: the question Thaler raised was narrower, and easier to settle cleanly, an image produced by the machine alone, with no human creative input in the result, and the program itself as the only claimed author. The threshold of human contribution that would be enough to ground a right in less clear-cut cases, an author who selects, arranges or retouches elements produced by a machine, remains unsettled after this case.

carte.punch: The Copyright Office says no: a machine cannot be the author of a work.
carte.idee: In 2019, the Copyright Office refuses to register an image whose only stated author is an artificial intelligence. Its Review Board upholds the refusal in 2022, the courts in 2023 and 2025, and the Supreme Court declines to review the case in 2026.

quiz.question: Why does the Copyright Office refuse to register the image A Recent Entrance to Paradise?
choix: Because the image reused, without permission, protected elements from other works
Because its only stated author was an artificial intelligence program, not a human being
Because Stephen Thaler had not paid the registration fees the Copyright Office requires
Because the image had already been published without a copyright notice before the application was filed
quiz.explication: The Copyright Office and the courts that uphold its refusal rely on a principle established for a century: only a human being can be an author under U.S. copyright law. Since Thaler named the Creativity Machine, and not himself, as the author, the image could not be registered.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What precedent does the Copyright Office rely on to refuse registration of the image?
choix: A federal law passed in 2019 to specifically govern works produced by artificial intelligence
An international agreement signed by the United States and the European Union on copyright protection
The 1884 precedent, Burrow-Giles Lithographic Co. v. Sarony, which defines the author as the source of the work
A 1998 decision on digital copyright applied to works published online
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Copyright Office's decision relies on the 1884 precedent, Burrow-Giles Lithographic Co. v. Sarony, in which the Supreme Court defines the author as the one to whom a work owes its origin.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Judge Beryl Howell write in her August 18, 2023 decision?
choix: That U.S. copyright law must now also apply to works produced by an AI
That Stephen Thaler must pay a fine for filing an application judged fraudulent
That a new federal law must be passed before the case can be decided
That human creativity is the sine qua non at the core of copyrightability
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Judge Beryl Howell writes in her August 18, 2023 decision that human creativity is the sine qua non at the core of copyrightability, upholding the refusal to register the image.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, what do none of the four decisions in this case settle?
choix: The threshold of human contribution that would be enough to ground a right in an AI-assisted work
Whether a Copyright Office decision can be appealed to the federal courts
The name of the machine Stephen Thaler used to produce the disputed image
The date on which Stephen Thaler filed his initial registration application
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry points out that none of the four decisions settles the threshold of human contribution that would be enough to ground a copyright when a person selects, arranges or retouches what a machine produced.
